title: Web Application Security: Thinking Like an Attacker

questions.question: The core defense against SQL injection is:
options: Parameterised queries / prepared statements — data never becomes code
questions.rationale: Parameterisation sends the query structure and the data separately, so an attacker's payload can only ever be compared as data, never executed as SQL.

questions.question: A stored XSS vulnerability means:
options: Attacker-supplied script is saved and later executed in other users' browsers
questions.rationale: A malicious payload persisted in a comment or profile runs in every visitor's session — the reason output must be escaped and CSP set.

questions.question: Which defense pairs with output escaping to stop XSS?
options: Content-Security-Policy restricting script sources (no inline scripts)
questions.rationale: CSP is defence in depth: even if escaping misses a context, the browser refuses to run scripts from unlisted origins.

questions.question: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) is best described as:
options: Changing an ID in a URL/API to access another user's record
questions.rationale: The server hands back object 1044 just because it was asked — the fix is verifying ownership/authorisation server-side on every request; UUIDs help but don't authorise.

questions.question: Which cookie flags protect a session cookie?
questions.rationale: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript (XSS) from reading it, Secure confines it to HTTPS, and SameSite blocks cross-site sends (CSRF).

questions.question: CSRF attacks are primarily mitigated by:
options: SameSite cookies plus per-form CSRF tokens
questions.rationale: CSRF abuses the browser auto-sending cookies cross-site; SameSite stops that, and tokens prove the request came from your own form. Note: CSRF tokens don't help against XSS.

questions.question: Passwords should be stored using:
options: A slow, salted hash like bcrypt or argon2
questions.rationale: Slow hashes with per-user salts make offline guessing astronomically expensive; MD5/SHA-1 are fast and collision-prone; encryption is for data you must read back — passwords aren't.

questions.question: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) is dangerous because:
options: The server can be tricked into fetching internal URLs (e.g., cloud metadata endpoints) on the attacker's behalf
questions.rationale: A URL-fetch feature becomes a pivot into the internal network — defences include allow-lists of destinations and blocking link-local/metadata addresses.

questions.question: 'Mass assignment' vulnerability refers to:
options: An API blindly copying user-submitted fields into an object — e.g., setting role: admin
questions.rationale: The fix is an allow-list of updatable fields; trusting the request body's shape lets attackers write to fields they should never touch.

questions.question: Which practice reflects 'defence in depth'?
options: Layering parameterised queries + least-privilege DB accounts + output escaping + CSP, so one failure isn't fatal
questions.rationale: Every layer will eventually fail; layered, independent controls ensure a single bypass doesn't become a full compromise.
